extracted.intended_audience: general readers, researchers, journalists, and policymakers interested in Albanian media
extracted.subtask_description: A country-level encyclopedic overview of the Albanian media system covering legal framework, regulators, ownership, funding, pluralism, public broadcaster, press freedom, and practical constraints such as censorship and journalist safety.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constitutional guarantees of freedom of speech and press
rubrics_metrics.description: The Constitution of Albania provides for freedom of speech and freedom of the press; it prohibits censorship and grants citizens the right to access information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although constitutionally guaranteed, the article notes that the government 'generally does not respect these rights in practice' and that the constitution and law also prohibit arbitrary interference with privacy, family, home, or correspondence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Right of access to information (statutory framework and implementation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Access to information is guaranteed by law since 1999; citizens have the right, in accordance with law, to acquire information on activities of state bodies and persons exercising public functions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implementation lags. A 2014 law aimed to prevent delays in officials' answers; institutions should appoint coordinators and a Commission for the Right to Information monitors compliance. Practical delays and weak enforcement are noted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Print press self-regulation and registration rules
rubrics_metrics.description: The print press in Albania is mostly self-regulated. The Law on the Press states 'The press is free. Freedom of the press is protected by law.' Printed publications do not require authorisation, nor are they registered in number at any time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This legal regime implies low prior-authorisation barriers for print, but self-regulation and market/ownership pressures still affect content and plurality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Electoral media coverage balance requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: During election campaigns, as stated by the Election Law, TV and radio coverage (but not the press) needs to be balanced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In practice the two main parties are allocated double the time of smaller parties. The Central Election Commission forms a Media Monitoring Board composed of party representatives (excluding smaller/newer parties) tasked with punishing non-compliant outlets with rather small fines — illustrating gaps between formal requirements and enforcement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Libel and defamation legal status
rubrics_metrics.description: Libel and defamation were decriminalised in March 2012 but remain punishable by high fines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: High fines are deemed to reinforce self-censorship among journalists. Since 2005 the government/public administration pledged not to sue journalists; since 2013 a Ministerial Code asks ministers not to sue without prime minister approval, but civil cases remain a concern.

rubrics_metrics.name: Online content criminal liability scope
rubrics_metrics.description: Online contents are lightly regulated; the only prosecuted contents are those concerning genocide or crimes against humanity, as well as provocation of ethnic, religious or other hate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Chief Prosecutor may and should collect all relevant content. Despite light regulation, other pressures (political, economic) affect online media. Separately, setting up a website requires a permit by the Authority on Electronic and Postal Communication (AKEP).

rubrics_metrics.name: Audiovisual Media Authority (AMA) regulatory role and composition
rubrics_metrics.description: The AMA is the main media regulator in Albania, tasked with issuing broadcasting licenses and monitoring their use. It is funded through fines, annual licences and fees, and can receive public budget money.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Members (5) are elected by Parliament for 5 years for max two terms; civil society proposes experts and MPs shortlist/elect (3 each); the chairman (7th member) is elected by Parliamentary majority. The article describes the AMA as 'commonly considered as highly politicised', noting parliamentary election/appointment procedures that risk politicisation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulatory independence and politicisation
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulatory bodies (AMA, NCRT, RTSH steering council) have appointment/election procedures involving Parliament and majorities, leading to concerns about politicisation and lack of independence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include contested AMA appointments, opposition boycotts, and OSCE remarks about RTSH coverage balance during elections. Independence deficits are linked to biased coverage and weakened enforcement of media pluralism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethical standards for journalists (Albanian Media Institute Code)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Ethical Code of the Albanian Media Institute (1996, revised 2006) states journalists 'have the right to obtain information, to publish, and to criticise. Information should be truthful, balanced and verified.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The code establishes normative standards for accuracy and balance; the article notes however that lack of resources, ownership pressure and weak labour conditions hinder adherence to these standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Journalists' labour conditions and professionalism
rubrics_metrics.description: The Albanian journalism labour market is unstable; many journalists work without contracts or for unpaid extra hours, face delayed salary payments, and lack job security.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poor labour conditions (90% without contracts per a 2012 study; low salaries) undermine motivation and security, push towards self-censorship or commercial/political interference, and reduce investigative journalism capability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Physical safety and risk of assault for journalists
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists in Albania remain at risk of being physically obstructed, assaulted or threatened while covering specific events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article cites incidents (e.g., 2014 attack on an A1 Report TV crew) demonstrating that threats and attacks contribute to self-censorship and reduced reporting on sensitive topics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Drivers of censorship and self-censorship
rubrics_metrics.description: Censorship and self-censorship are present and originate from political and economic pressures, lack of financial viability for media outlets, and lack of professionalism, ethics and respect for journalists’ rights.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ownership links between media, business and politics, state-sponsored advertising, big advertisers, owners’ economic/political interests, and lack of physical/job security are named as main drivers. Survey data (BIRN) indicate editorial lines are often influenced by such factors, producing one-sided coverage and avoidance of topics like politics, organised crime and economy.

rubrics_metrics.name: State-media financial relations and state advertising opacity
rubrics_metrics.description: The law does not regulate state aid for the media, and opacity in allocation of state advertising is a persistent controversy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reported examples include substantial state advertising channeled to single groups favourable to the government and municipal-level allocation practices that biased distribution. Lack of regulation/transparency in state funds fosters clientelism and editorial influence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Media funding model and economic vulnerability
rubrics_metrics.description: Albanian media are mainly funded through advertising revenues, sponsorships and the sale of media productions; economic crisis reduced broadcasters' advertising share making outlets reliant on owners' direct financing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reduced advertising revenues (e.g., drop from 58% to 30% for broadcasters between 2009–2010) increase vulnerability to business and political interference, reduce capacity for investigative journalism and professional development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency of media ownership and reporting requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Transparency of media ownership is low; media outlets must register to the National Registration Centre declaring shareholders (so ownership data are available for most outlets), but electronic media are not obliged to register there. Online media must report ownership changes to the National Council of Radio Television (NCRT), but the NCRT register is not available online and is accessible only upon request.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Digitisation has improved availability for some sectors, but doubts persist whether declared owners are the actual owners; regulators are not obliged to publish collected data and reporting of financial balances is inconsistent (e.g., only 25% submitted balances in 2012), limiting public scrutiny.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concentration and cross-ownership regulation (scope and gaps)
rubrics_metrics.description: Concentration is a growing concern: consolidation via same editorial groups across platforms is common; cross-ownership rules in the Law on Audiovisual Media cover radio and TV but do not cover print, leaving gaps.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ownership concentration is obscured by proxies, rotation of family/trusted persons in formal positions, creation of multiple companies, and limited enforcement. Foreign investors are present but have not eliminated problems of hidden ownership and cross-ownership of platforms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public service broadcaster obligations (RTSH)
rubrics_metrics.description: RTSH should 'promote Albanian culture and language, and artistic and literary creativity'; produce and broadcast freely accessible content related to national health, public order, and emergencies. Original content should amount to 50% of broadcasts; RTSH broadcasts in minority languages in border regions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: RTSH is funded via a license fee (€0.75/month per family) and may receive advertising and other revenues. Steering Council appointment procedures mirror AMA and raise independence/politicisation concerns; OSCE noted balance problems during elections and RTSH typically shows pro-government bias.

rubrics_metrics.name: Licensing and financial oversight requirements for broadcasters
rubrics_metrics.description: When granting licences to broadcast media, the regulator asks for proofs that the outlet holds a certain level of capital, and broadcast operators are supposed to submit annual balances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The origin of capital is not checked; annual balances submitted to tax offices are confidential and submission to the regulator is non-compulsory (only a small percentage comply), undermining financial transparency and enabling hidden ownership/funding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirements for establishment/registration of online media
rubrics_metrics.description: Setting up a website requires a permit by the Authority on Electronic and Postal Communication (AKEP). Online media must report ownership data and changes to the NCRT, though the register is not publicly online.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although online media offer independent alternatives, they often lack resources and reach smaller audiences; regulatory/permitting requirements and limited transparency of registers affect accountability.
